newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN EXPORT INCENTIVES COULD DIVERT FUNDS.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN EXPORT INCENTIVES COULD DIVERT FUNDS.

text.p: South Africa's parliamentary trade and industry committee has expressed concern about the effect of export incentives on government coffers and whether it was getting value for money for specialist studies.

In its report on the Department of Trade and Industry's 1997/98 budget, the committee said that although the General Export Incentive Scheme (GEIS) would be phased out at the end of this year, it could still divert funds that could be used for more urgent needs.
GEIS is estimated to account for 34.7 percent of the department's total three billion rand budget this year, down from 48.6 percent in 1996/97.
The committee said it was concerned about the open-ended nature of GEIS payments.
"Qualifying businesses have a right to these payments whether or not sufficient funds have been budgeted," it said.

It was aware that the department was concerned that the growth in manufactured exports could create a situation where claims exceeded the budgeted amount, and where GEIS payments considerably reduced funds which should be deployed for supply side programmes.
The committee said it would support moves by government, business and labour to address this issue through their tri-partite negotiating forum, the National Economic Development and Labour Council.

It was also concerned about the efficiency of, and the extent to which government was getting value for money from a number of new programmes, including cluster studies, tax incentives and small business support programmes.
"The committee appreciates the importance of each of these, but is aware that existing programmes in these areas have had mixed results and are being refined to improve delivery," it said.

It would also like a clearer indication of how the department's various programmes were affecting employment levels. It was aware that this might be difficult to measure, but said some criteria for measuring progress was urgently needed.
The committee was also concerned about the effect that voluntary severance packages for senior staff was having on skills levels within the department.
